titre: Predictors of improvement in personal recovery and activity engagement among mental health service users following a group-based sensory modulation intervention.
auteurs: Forsberg Klara, Sutton Daniel, Stjernswärd Sigrid, Bejerholm Ulrika, Argentzell Elisabeth
resume: Mental health service users often have sensory processing difficulties affecting activity engagement and personal recovery. Since interventions targeting this area are scarce, a group-based sensory modulation intervention was developed. To determine in which settings and for whom this intervention has clinical value, this study aimed to investigate whether sociodemographic and clinical baseline characteristics were associated with improvement in personal recovery and activity engagement. This study included participants from the intervention group (N = 107) of a trial (reg.nr: NCT06432114) evaluating an 11-week group-based sensory modulation intervention in mental health outpatient units. Data were collected at baseline, post-intervention, and at 6-month follow-up. Analysis included descriptive statistics and baseline-adjusted multiple linear regression models. Results showed that the absence of a psychosis diagnosis was associated with a higher mean score of personal recovery at post-intervention (p = 0.003), but not at 6-months follow-up (p = 0.826). There were no significant associations between the predictors and activity engagement. Most predictors in the models were not significantly associated with improvement across any of the outcomes. This suggests that improvement in personal recovery and activity engagement, following the intervention, was accessible to the diverse group of mental health service users, independent of their baseline characteristics.

titre: Assessing the Willingness of Future Health Care Providers to Participate in Vaccine Trials: Cross-Sectional VACCELERATE European Study.
auteurs: Yiallouris Andreas, Filippou Charalampos, Merakou Christina, Argyropoulos Christos D, Themistocleous Sophia C, Shiamakkides George, Sarantopoulos Andreas, Shaikh Ahmed Razi, Noula Evgenia, Nearchou Andria, Johnson Elizabeth O, Papaconstantinou-Leontidou Maria, Armeftis Charis, Astras George, Stewart Fiona A, Albus Kerstin, Salmanton-García Jon, Leckler Janina, Azzini Anna Maria, Davis Ruth Joanna, Součková Lenka, Askling Helena H, Battle Tobias Lindström, Álvarez-Barco Elena, Mozeryte Augustina, Poulimeneas Dimitrios, Kopsidas Ioannis, Prellezo Jana Baranda, Valdenmaiier Olena, Jakobsen Stine F, Cox Rebecca Jane, Hellemans Margot, Hendrickx Greet, van Damme Pierre, Ochando Jordi, Zaoutis Theoklis E, Jancoriene Ligita, Mallon Patrick, Nauclér Pontus, Husa Petr, Tacconelli Evelina, Cornely Oliver A, Pana Zoi-Dorothea
resume: Future health professionals are expected to recommend vaccines, communicate with patients about vaccine safety, and support clinical trial literacy and recruitment during public health emergencies. However, their own willingness to participate in vaccine trials, and the barriers that shape that willingness, remain incompletely characterized across Europe. This study aimed to assess willingness to participate in future vaccine trials among European students in health-related disciplines and to describe their perceived barriers, motivations, vaccine attitudes, and preferred sources of health information. We conducted an open, multilingual, cross-sectional web survey within the VACCELERATE network from June to November 2023. National coordinators distributed the survey through institutional mailing lists, student associations, and program channels in participating European countries. Eligible participants were students aged 18 years or older enrolled in medicine, dentistry, nursing, pharmacy, psychology, biomedical sciences, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, or other health-related programs. The questionnaire assessed demographic characteristics, primary sources of health information, vaccine attitudes, willingness to participate in future vaccine trials, barriers among unwilling or unsure respondents, and motivations for participation. Analyses were descriptive, and denominators varied by item because nonmandatory questions could be skipped. Of 1381 eligible respondents, 1192 (86.3%) answered the primary willingness question: 32.9% (n=392) were willing to participate in a future vaccine trial, 38.8% (n=463) were unsure, and 28.3% (n=337) were unwilling. Among the 769 respondents who were unwilling or unsure and selected barriers, the most frequent concerns were potential side effects (n=574, 74.6%) and not wanting to be a "test subject" (n=276, 35.9%). Among 1289 respondents included in the motivation analysis, commonly selected motivators included knowing the risks and side effects involved (n=575, 44.6%), becoming part of the solution to an important health problem (n=584, 45.3%), and knowing that personal safety would be protected (n=500, 38.8%). In this multicountry European sample of health professional students, only one-third reported willingness to participate in future vaccine trials, while the largest group was unsure. The findings suggest that trial-readiness initiatives for future health professionals should prioritize transparent communication about safety monitoring, risks and side effects, participant protections, and the practical conduct of vaccine trials. Because recruitment used an open convenience approach, the results should be interpreted as exploratory and hypothesis generating rather than representative of all European health professional students.

titre: The Effectiveness of Digital Collage Activity Based on a Life Review for Home-Dwelling Older Patients With Cancer and Their Families: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
auteurs: Sakaguchi Satoko, Kaneko Fumiko, Saita Kazuya, Okamura Hitoshi
revue: The American journal of hospice & palliative care
resume: PurposeThis study aimed to develop and implement digital collage activity based on a life review, a psychosocial support tool for patients with cancer, and investigate its preliminary effectiveness for patients and their families.MethodsThis randomized controlled trial assigned 42 participants to intervention and control groups (21 per group). The intervention group participated in three sessions (life review, activity, and review) over approximately 10 days. The control group completed the questionnaire at the same three time points as the intervention group (pre-intervention, post-intervention, and 1 week later). Data were analyzed using covariance analysis, with performance status as a covariate and the Self-Efficacy Scale for Terminal Cancer as the dependent variable. Data from family members were analyzed using a two-way analysis of variance, with the Caregiver Quality of Life Index-Cancer (CQOLC) as the dependent variable.Major FindingsThirteen participants in the intervention group and 16 in the control group completed the program. In the intervention group, significant interactions were observed between the total self-efficacy score and the Symptom Coping Efficacy and Affect Regulation Efficacy subscales. In the family intervention group, significant interactions were observed for the total CQOLC score, and significant changes were noted in the psychological burden subscales. However, no significant differences were observed between the two groups on self-esteem and depression scales for either patients or family members.ConclusionsThese findings suggest that digital collage activity based on a life review has the potential to improve psychosocial self-efficacy among patients and quality of life among family caregivers.

titre: The Feasibility of Using Virtual Reality With Debriefing as a Treatment Modality for Chronic Pain.
auteurs: Baker Nancy A, Baird Joanne, Kenney Megan, Ortiz Kaley, Wasan Ajay D
revue: The American journal of occupational therapy : official publication of the American Occupational Therapy Association
resume: ImportanceChronic pain is a leading cause of disability. Traditional rehabilitation approaches may not produce meaningful functional improvement, necessitating innovative approaches.ObjectiveTo assess the feasibility and acceptability of integrating fully immersive virtual reality (FIVR) and debriefing into occupational therapy (OT) for chronic pain management. We hypothesized that FIVR plus debriefing (IVRSOT) would improve pain, fear of movement, and confidence compared to standard OT (SOT).DesignIn this mixed methods feasibility study, participants were randomized to SOT or IVRSOT. Data were analyzed using nonparametric statistics and content analysis.SettingOutpatient interdisciplinary pain clinic using a biopsychosocial model.ParticipantsAdults with chronic pain, with 31 enrolled and 16 having data suitable for analysis.Outcomes and MeasuresPain intensity, pain interference, kinesiophobia, self-efficacy, and social functioning were assessed using validated tools.ResultsIVRSOT participants showed significant improvement in pain self-efficacy, fatigue, and pain interference, accompanied by a decline in physical function; between group comparisons for physical function and social role participation favored SOT. Qualitative data revealed enhanced engagement, insight, and functional carryover.Conclusion and RelevanceFIVR with debriefing is a feasible and engaging approach for chronic pain intervention, with the potential to enhance self-efficacy and functional outcomes.

titre: Outpatient occupational therapy access for rural stroke survivors: barriers as perceived by therapists.
auteurs: Stevens Emily A, Pfeifer Lexie J, Malcolm Matt P
resume: Identify occupational therapist (OTs) perceived barriers to occupational therapy (OT) access for rural stroke survivors as well as barriers in stroke specific training of therapists. An electronic gap analysis survey was developed and distributed via email. Twenty-six OTs responded. Responses were analyzed utilizing descriptive statistics and summarization of comments. Therapist-perceived barriers included: family/caregiver support, distance to clinic, insurance coverage, health literacy, roles and responsibilities, financial, and transportation. The primary barrier in treating rural stroke survivors identified by OTs was lack of appropriate clinic equipment for neuro-specific interventions. Further research is needed in a larger sample size to explore the extent to which therapist-perceived barriers agree with the stroke survivor's perspective and facilitate solutions to overcome them.

titre: Therapeutic Climbing in Pediatric Practice: Therapist Perspectives on Mechanisms, Delivery, and Contextual Factors - A Qualitative Study.
auteurs: Kaar Carmen, Kopp Martin
resume: Therapeutic climbing is increasingly used in pediatric occupational therapy, yet implementation practices and reasons for non‑adoption remain underexplored. This qualitative study examined how Austrian pediatric occupational therapists position therapeutic climbing within occupation‑centered, movement‑based practice; how they deliver it in community contexts; perceived benefits and mechanisms; and barriers to adoption, including non‑user perspectives. Semi‑structured interviews were conducted with 24 state‑certified pediatric occupational therapy practitioners (12 climbing users, 12 non‑users) and analyzed inductively using reflexive thematic analysis. Therapists described therapeutic climbing as a structured, safety‑oriented, movement‑based occupational therapy intervention delivered in individual, dyadic, and small‑group formats, typically progressing from separation and everyday task preparation through warm‑up to graded climbing, with explicit readiness criteria for height and rope work under high supervision. Belaying was used as closely overseen responsibility training. Reported benefits co‑occurred across domains: motor coordination and praxis, sensory regulation, attention and other executive functions, self‑efficacy, social responsibility, and strong motivation linked to therapeutic climbing's sport‑like framing in real‑world settings. Therapists attributed these effects to belay‑based trust and responsibility, graded exposure to height, dense problem‑solving with immediate feedback, visible progress, and ecological delivery in public gyms. Adoption depended on accepting facility partners, intensive logistics and training, safety/liability governance, and uncovered venue costs. Non‑users largely endorsed therapeutic climbing's rationale but cited lack of personal climbing practice, limited gym access, training and safety demands, and unreimbursed fees. Overall, therapeutic climbing was viewed as a promising, participation‑oriented approach; principal constraints were systemic rather than conceptual. Rigorous comparative studies with clear fidelity and context reporting are needed to identify mechanisms and specify for whom and under what conditions therapeutic climbing adds value.

titre: An Occupational Therapy Perspective on Environmental Interventions for Community-Dwelling People With Dementia: A Scoping Review.
auteurs: Do Jihye, Yoo Ingyu
revue: The American journal of occupational therapy : official publication of the American Occupational Therapy Association
resume: ImportanceEnvironmental interventions support "aging in place" for people with dementia. However, the specific roles of occupational therapists within multidisciplinary teams providing these interventions require systematic mapping to clarify their value.ObjectiveTo map characteristics of multidisciplinary environmental interventions for community-dwelling people with dementia and clarify specific occupational therapy roles.Data SourcesPubMed, CINAHL, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect were searched for peer-reviewed studies (January 2010-July 2025).Study Selection and Data CollectionFollowing JBI and PRISMA-ScR guidelines, two reviewers independently selected studies and charted data on multidisciplinary environmental interventions.FindingsSeventeen studies were included, featuring interventions like home modifications and technology-based programs. Occupational therapists primarily conducted functional and environmental assessments, utilized person-environment-occupation perspectives for intervention planning, and facilitated multidisciplinary team processes. Key outcomes included functional performance, fall risk, and caregiver measures.Conclusions and RelevanceOccupational therapists crucially link functional abilities with environmental conditions. This review highlights their contributions while identifying gaps in how multidisciplinary collaboration and occupational therapy roles are operationalized and reported.

titre: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis on the Effectiveness of Horticultural Therapy in Cancer Survivors.
auteurs: Obembe Adebimpe, Alfaro Liliana, Wong Haylie, Shelite Anna, Smith Mary, Chipy Nicole
revue: The American journal of occupational therapy : official publication of the American Occupational Therapy Association
resume: ImportanceCommon cancer treatments can produce side effects that interfere with daily functioning. In contrast, nature-based therapies such as horticultural therapy may support physical function, psychosocial well-being, and lifestyle behaviors, thereby promoting occupational engagement and quality of life.ObjectiveTo determine the effectiveness of garden-based horticultural therapy among cancer survivors.Data SourcesSearches were conducted in Academic Search Complete, ProQuest, JSTOR, CINAHL Complete, PubMed, Psychology and Behavioral Sciences Collection, American Journal of Occupational Therapy, and Journal of the American Medical Association, as well as reference lists from relevant reviews and full-text articles.Study Selection and Data CollectionThe review followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines and included primary intervention studies published within the past 10 years that examined soil-based garden interventions for adult cancer survivors.FindingsEight studies involving 634 participants were included in the review and three in the meta-analysis. Intervention duration ranged from 6 weeks to 1 year. Seven studies reported increased fruit and vegetable intake, whereas pain remained unchanged in five studies. Findings for psychosocial well-being and physical functioning were mixed. Three randomized controlled trials demonstrated significant pooled effects for physical health outcomes (standardized mean difference [SMD] = -0.38, 95% confidence interval [CI] = [-0.62, -0.13], Z = 3.02), physical performance (SMD = 0.19, 95% CI = [0.01 to 0.37], Z = 2.10), and lifestyle behaviors (SMD = 0.67, 95% CI = [0.27 to 1.06], Z = 3.32). No significant effect was found for psychosocial health outcomes.Conclusions and RelevanceThese preliminary findings suggest that garden-based horticultural therapy may support improvements in physical functioning and lifestyle behaviors among cancer survivors, though rigorous controlled trials are needed to confirm efficacy. Horticultural therapy warrants consideration as a complementary component of comprehensive occupation-based care to promote meaningful occupational engagement in this population.

titre: Treatment Fidelity of AquOTic: An Occupational Therapy-Based Aquatic Intervention for Children on the Autism Spectrum.
auteurs: Kemp Erika, Yates Savanna, Quincy Lauren, Watson-Grace Amy, Crasta Jewel
revue: The American journal of occupational therapy : official publication of the American Occupational Therapy Association
resume: ImportanceChildren on the autism spectrum face significantly higher risks for unintentional drowning, yet aquatic interventions often lack the standardized specification necessary for evidence-based replication.ObjectiveTo examine the treatment fidelity of AquOTic.DesignDescriptive design based on a larger randomized controlled trial.SettingCounty Board of Developmental Disabilities therapy pool.ParticipantsChildren on the autism spectrum (N = 37) ages 5 to 9 year and graduate-level therapy students (swim buddies, N = 18).InterventionAquOTic is a manualized 10-week occupational therapy-based water competency intervention for children on the autism spectrum.Outcomes and MeasuresAdherence was measured via a 13-item fidelity self-checklist and video-coding analysis.ResultsHigh overall fidelity was achieved, with mean swim buddy adherence at 95.93%. Component-level fidelity averaged 97.36%, with core ingredients such as play-based strategies, modeling, and water property integration consistently appearing in 100% of analyzed sessions.Conclusions and RelevanceThe AquOTic intervention demonstrates high treatment fidelity, confirming that theorized active ingredients are consistently implemented. Use of fidelity practices and intervention specification supports the reproducibility and clinical translation of occupational therapy-led aquatic interventions to improve water safety for autistic children.

titre: 'Some of Them Were Created by People Who Have Never Had a Stroke': Understanding Desired Physical and Occupational Therapy Research Study Features for People With Chronic Stroke.
auteurs: Schwab-Farrell Sarah M, Ficke Jasmine, Pressler Daria, Farrell Kelly, Rose Becca, Miller Valerie
revue: Health expectations : an international journal of public participation in health care and health policy
resume: People with stroke have historically had limited involvement in physical and occupational therapy research studies. Scientists and funders, rather than those most affected by the outcomes of research, largely make decisions about what studies should focus on. When research is not informed by the lived experiences of people with disability, researchers may ask the wrong questions or make incorrect assumptions about disability. The purpose of this study was to identify desired features and characteristics for physical and occupational therapy research studies, from the perspective of people with chronic stroke. We completed four iterative focus group discussions with a small group of adults with chronic stroke. The group was purposively sampled to ensure a range of prior stroke research experiences and stroke-related impairments. Thematic analysis was conducted on discussion content to identify desired study features. Four major desired study features were constructed: (1) Desire for relationships; (2) Understand the purpose; (3) Capability-oriented; and (4) Focused on individual participation needs. Participants expressed a desire for physical and occupational therapy studies to focus on what they can do (rather than what they cannot do) while also embracing the heterogeneity of stroke presentation. Studies involving elements of stroke community support and an understanding of potential benefits or information about stroke are also desired. Collaborative research design can contribute to future research that is authentic and valuable to people with lived experience while concurrently lessening harmful disability narratives that are often unintentionally maintained by non-disabled researchers. By working with a group of adults with chronic stroke, we were able to identify valued study features that can be incorporated into future stroke research studies. Individuals with lived experience of stroke engaged in the discussions presented in this paper to collaboratively identify desired stroke study features. People with stroke were also involved in the developing interpretation of the presented data and reviewed the final version of the manuscript.

titre: Functional Neurological Disorder Management in a Pediatric Hospital: A Retrospective Chart Review.
auteurs: Rettig Mateya, Sweetland Nicole, Shao Yanhao, Thompson Laurie, Brown Laurey, Norwood Meredith
resume: Functional neurological disorder (FND) is a complex, multinetwork brain disorder that is characterized by the presence of a broad range of neurological symptoms in the absence of neurological disease or damage. For pediatric patients requiring an in-patient stay, misdiagnosis, lack of provider consistency and diagnostic education, frequent testing and work-up, and invasive procedures are often reported. This review will characterize the population, identify current state for receiving diagnosis, detect variability in service delivery, and provide information to evaluate use of resources. This retrospective chart review examined electronic medical records (EMRs) of 59 patients at a pediatric teaching hospital who were admitted following a visit to the emergency department. Records were compiled by the rehabilitation department with inclusion criteria as having a documented diagnosis of FND or as having a similar functional movement related diagnosis such as chorea, panic disorder, and psychogenic nonepileptic seizure (PNES). Extracted data included the following: demographics, patient characteristics, admission characteristics and experience, and discharge recommendations. Fifty-nine charts were initially reviewed with 57 meeting inclusion criteria. The subjects in this study had a mean age of 13.7 years (SD: 6.33) and 80.7% were female. The most commonly reported psychiatric diagnoses included anxiety (66.7%), ADHD (29.6%), and depression (22.2%). The most commonly reported FND symptoms at admission were weakness (47.4%), gait instability (28.1%), sensory disturbances (26.3%), and tremor (19.1%). Physical therapy consultations were the most frequently performed (66.7%), followed by occupational therapy (52.6%), psychiatry (38.6%), and psychology (5.3%). No interdisciplinary care conferences were performed. The mean length of stay was 5.13 days (SD: 4.45 days). Readmission rate after 30 days was 16.5%. This retrospective EMR review identifies opportunities to improve care for pediatric FND, including reducing unnecessary imaging, testing, and readmissions through strengthened provider, patient, and family education. Findings also highlight inconsistent referrals to physical therapy, occupational therapy, and mental health services. Addressing these gaps may enhance patient experience, support more coordinated interdisciplinary care, and reduce healthcare utilization for this under-recognized population.

titre: From data entry to digital transformation: Allied health perspectives on standardised electronic medical records data.
auteurs: Schwarz Maria, Ward Elizabeth C, Jeffery Sarah, Simmons Joshua, Perkins Kristy, Juffs Philip, Burrett Sara
revue: Health information management : journal of the Health Information Management Association of Australia
resume: Electronic medical records (EMRs) currently rely on standardised data fields to support secondary data use for clinical care, performance monitoring, and system-level reporting. However, utilisation of standardised data capture and reporting within allied health remains underdeveloped in practice. Greater understanding of how allied health clinicians and managers perceive the purpose, value, and impact of standardised data collection is needed to support advancement in data maturity and transformation of utilisation. To explore the perceived benefits, challenges and future opportunities of standardised data collection within an EMR, from the allied health perspective. A qualitative descriptive study using semi-structured interviews was conducted with 28 allied health clinicians and managers from 5 allied health disciplines: Dietetics, Occupational Therapy, Physiotherapy, Speech Pathology, and Social Work. Five overarching themes reflected a gap between the acknowledged value of standardised data collection and its current utilisation in allied health practice: (i) Recognised value but unrealised potential of EMR data, including its role in clinical insights, service planning, financial justification, and professional advocacy; (ii) System and workflow misalignment limits meaningful data use, including disconnect between data collection and use, workflow burden, inefficient data capture, system constraints; (iii) Standardisation as both enabler and constraint, supporting benchmarking and system alignment while limiting clinical flexibility and contextual relevance; (iv) Pathways to advancing data maturity, including training, improved data and digital literacy, and integration with emerging technologies; and the broader impact of (v) Digital workflows reshaping workforce and care delivery, with implications for team-based and person-centred care. While standardised EMR data were recognised as valuable, their potential remains limited when data collection is poorly aligned with allied health workflows. Advancing allied health data maturity requires clinically meaningful, workflow-integrated and feedback-driven approaches that improve usability while supporting high-quality data for secondary use.Implication for health information management practice:Standardisation efforts must balance data quality with clinical relevance, ensuring data collection aligns with real-world workflows and supports meaningful use.

titre: Occupational Justice PLUS: From theoretical salience to practical application-An analysis of community narratives from a bushfire event.
auteurs: Huppatz Eliza, McKinstry Carol, Whiteford Gail, George Emma
resume: Emerging scholarship highlights the dominance of Western epistemologies in disaster research, limiting diversity and participation in knowledge production. The occupational therapy profession faces similar critiques of epistemic and hegemonic blind spots, prompting calls for critical reflection on professional assumptions. Drawing on narratives and guided by Whiteford's Occupational Justice PLUS model, we explore how learnings from community members' responses to a bushfire event could broaden our understanding of occupational, epistemic, and hermeneutic justice in the context of disasters and, more broadly, other injustices. This qualitative study used a phenomenological hermeneutical approach to explore narratives of disaster recovery. Data included a written narrative from 'Doing Our Best' and the film 'We Are Conjola'. Analysis followed Lindseth and Norberg's three-step process: naïve reading, structural analysis of themes, and comprehensive interpretation informed by literature and theories. Findings revealed interconnected injustices. Occupational injustice arose from restricted access to resources during bushfire response and recovery, with community-led initiatives critical to restoring occupational justice. Epistemic injustice was evident in government disregard for climate science and Indigenous knowledge, compounded by media erasure, prompting the community to create its own narrative through film. Hermeneutic injustice occurred when aspects of social identity were obscured from collective understanding; residents responded through artistic expression to reclaim identity, share lived experience, and communicate systemic failures. Community-driven action addressed occupational, epistemic, and hermeneutic injustices following the Conjola bushfire. These findings highlight the relevance of the Occupational Justice PLUS model for disaster contexts, emphasising the need for occupational therapists to adopt critical, justice-oriented approaches that privilege community voice and foster community-led action in disaster recovery and knowledge creation. Advocacy for community voice and future research on applying the Occupational Justice PLUS model are essential to support inclusive, community-driven recovery and strengthen knowledge creation in disaster contexts.

titre: Audiology Workforce Supply and Population Demand: Trends, Benchmarks, and Implications.
auteurs: Bray Victor, Amlani Amyn M
resume: Audiology's viability as a self-sustaining, autonomous profession depends on a workforce capable of meeting population demand. This article benchmarks audiology's (AuD) workforce supply against comparable healthcare professions and projected growth in hearing loss prevalence. Using Bureau of Labor Statistics data from 1999 to 2024, AuD workforce trends were compared with 16 other advanced-degree healthcare professions. AuD's mean annual growth rate (1.77%) ranked third lowest among 17 master's- and doctoral-level professions, well below four peer disciplines (occupational therapy, physical therapy, optometry, speech-language pathology), which grew 5.5 times faster over the same period. An input/output model of graduate production versus workforce departure showed that AuD's constrained growth stems not from insufficient educational throughput but from elevated departure rates, including abandonment of the profession. Meanwhile, the hearing aid specialist workforce grew over 200% between 2012 and 2024, suggesting substitution in core clinical functions. Population modeling projects the number of U.S. adults with hearing impairment will nearly double by 2060, widening the supply-demand gap. These findings indicate that AuD's transition to a doctoral entry-level degree introduced a lasting structural constraint on workforce capacity, with implications for access to care, professional autonomy, and audiology's positioning within value-based healthcare delivery.

titre: Early occupational therapy use of a 3D printer introduced with minimal formal support: a single-site pre-post observational study.
auteurs: Harada Yusuke, Sawada Yuki, Momma Hiroshi, Takeshima Rie, Suzurikawa Jun
resume: Three-dimensional (3D) printers can produce customized assistive devices in occupational therapy; however, occupational therapists' perceptions and early usage following clinical introduction remain poorly understood. This study examined perceptions, perceived barriers and enabling conditions, and early usage patterns among occupational therapists following 3D printer introduction in a rehabilitation hospital with minimal formal implementation support. A 3D printer was installed in the occupational therapy department, allowing trial printing of existing design data after brief basic instruction was provided to one representative therapist; no structured staff training, CAD instruction, formal usage recommendations, workflow integration, or dedicated institutional support was provided. A self-administered study-specific, non-validated questionnaire assessed perceptions and selected implementation-related conditions before and six months after installation. Paired data from 43 participants (follow-up rate: 79.6%) were analyzed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank and McNemar tests. After installation, selection of the barrier "there is no 3D printer in the workplace" significantly decreased (adjusted p < 0.001), whereas selection of institutional and operational constraints, including insufficient time (adjusted p < 0.001) and lack of medical reimbursement (adjusted p = 0.044), increased. Participants showed less agreement that using a 3D printer was difficult (adjusted p = 0.047), while agreement that 3D printing was useful in occupational therapy practice also decreased (adjusted p = 0.044). Although statistically significant, these changes were small in magnitude. No statistically significant change was observed in future intention to use 3D printing (adjusted p = 0.063). Available printer records did not permit quantitative assessment of individual use; use remained limited to exploratory printing of existing designs. The introduction of a printer with minimal formal support was not accompanied by clear progression toward routine clinical use during the six-month observation period. These exploratory findings support further evaluation of structured education, technical assistance, workflow integration, and institutional arrangements, but do not establish their effectiveness or the causal effect of printer availability.

titre: Sensory-Strength Training Improves Postural Balance and Working Memory in Children With Dyslexia.
auteurs: Belhaj Yassin, Laatar Rabeb, Harrabi Mohammed Achraf, Borji Rihab, Rebai Haithem, Sahli Sonia
resume: This randomized controlled trial examined the effects of combined sensory and strength training (SST) on postural balance and working memory in children with dyslexia. Twenty-nine dyslexic children (six females/23 males; mean age: 9.79 ± 1.44 years) were assigned to three groups: a SST group, a strength training group, and a control group. The intervention lasted 6 weeks, comprising three sessions per week, with each session lasting 45-60 min. Preassessment and postassessments included measures of postural balance and working memory, with muscle strength evaluated as a secondary outcome. After training, postural balance improved significantly (p < .001) only in the SST group. Moreover, both training groups showed significant improvements in working memory (p < .001) and muscle strength (p < .001) compared with baseline. The SST intervention could be integrated into school-based physical education programs or occupational therapy sessions to support motor and cognitive development in dyslexic children.

titre: Influence of Immersion Level and Game Type on Virtual Reality Interventions for Upper Limb Function After Stroke: Protocol for a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
auteurs: da Silva Dayenne Jeneffer Souza, Cunha Vitor Leandro da, Farias Luanna Barbara de Araújo, Carlos Lara Cecília de Araújo, Medeiros Candice Simões Pimenta de, Vieira Edgar Ramos, Cavalcanti Fabrícia Azevedo da Costa
resume: Upper limb impairment is a common consequence of stroke, affecting independence and quality of life. Virtual reality (VR) interventions, including serious games designed for therapeutic purposes and commercial games developed primarily for entertainment, have been increasingly used for poststroke upper limb rehabilitation. Evidence comparing the effectiveness of these game types on functional outcomes remains unclear. This systematic review protocol aims to determine whether serious and commercial VR games differentially impact upper limb function, measured by the Action Research Arm Test, in adults after stroke. Secondary outcomes will include upper limb motor function assessed using the Fugl-Meyer Assessment-Upper Extremity, Box and Block Test, Motor Activity Log, Jebsen-Taylor Hand Function Test, and Wolf Motor Function Test; functional independence assessed using the Functional Independence Measure and Barthel index; and adherence indicators, including dropout rates and session completion. Secondary objectives include evaluating pooled VR effects vs conventional therapy (CT) and exploring potential moderators, such as VR immersion level and stroke chronicity. Parallel randomized controlled trials involving adults (aged ≥18 years) with ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke in the acute, subacute, or chronic phases will be included. Interventions using serious or commercial VR games (nonimmersive, semi-immersive, or fully immersive) delivered alone or combined with CT will be considered. Studies using nongamified VR, digital technologies without VR, or augmented reality not integrated into VR will be excluded. Eligible comparators include conventional physiotherapy, occupational therapy, usual care, educational interventions, or no therapy. This protocol was developed in accordance with the PRISMA-P (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses-Protocols) guidelines. Systematic searches will be conducted in the PubMed (MEDLINE), Web of Science, Embase, Scopus, Virtual Health Library, ScienceDirect, Physiotherapy Evidence Database, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, ClinicalTrials.gov, Brazilian Clinical Trials Registry, World Health Organization (WHO) International Clinical Trial Registry Platform, and ISRCTN Registry databases from inception to February 2026. Data extraction will be performed independently by 2 reviewers, and risk of bias will be assessed using the Cochrane risk of bias 2.0 tool. Meta-analyses will be conducted when clinical and methodological homogeneity permits. A random-effects model is planned; however, the final choice of model will be based on the level of heterogeneity observed at the time of analysis. Subgroup analyses will explore stroke phase, immersion level, intervention dosage, and concomitant therapy. Data collection is planned from inception to February 2026. Study screening and data extraction are ongoing, with synthesis and meta-analysis expected by November 2026 and final publication anticipated in winter 2026. This systematic review will clarify whether different VR game formats produce distinct effects on upper limb rehabilitation after stroke, providing evidence to inform the design and implementation of VR-based neurorehabilitation interventions. PROSPERO CRD42024595266; https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD42024595266. DERR1-10.2196/95135.

titre: Teaching Social Inequities in Canadian Occupational Therapy: Tensions and Strategies for an 'Embedded Sociologist'.
auteurs: Beagan Brenda L
resume: Health professions education increasingly addresses social inequities, cultivating student awareness of structured power relations. Yet such teaching is met with resistance, with students prioritizing "hard" sciences and demanding immediate relevance and clinical application for everything taught. Sociological teaching and pedagogies are too often dismissed as "fluffy" and "wasting time." In Canada, professional competencies in occupational therapy now require practitioners to engage in anti-oppressive practice, which means education programs need to teach those skills. This article employs an autoethnographic approach to critically reflect on 25 years of teaching about social inequities in occupational therapy. Four challenges arise: 1. Epistemological dissonance, with objectivity and individualism deeply unsettled by sociological thinking; 2. Insistence on immediate relevance and application, which can lead to a problematic reliance on first-voices guests; 3. Simultaneous privilege and absence-of-privilege in the classroom, alongside a "charitable model" rescuing stance; and 4. The importance of emotion in learning difficult topics. A pedagogy of discomfort invites learners to stay present to the unsettling emotions that may arise as they confront systemic social power relations. This means moving away from notions of "safe" classrooms toward emphasizing courage in the face of complex feelings. Helplessness and powerlessness may be countered through cultivating critical hope, as a necessary step toward social change.

titre: Etiological Diagnoses Versus Descriptive Developmental Diagnoses.
auteurs: Moran Elisa J, Kelsey Sophia, Salman Shahad, Voigt Robert G
revue: Journal of developmental and behavioral pediatrics : JDBP
resume: Jane is a 7-year-old girl who presented for a developmental-behavioral pediatrics (DBP) evaluation because of parental concern about developmental delays and atypical behavior. Jane is a former term infant who was small for gestational age. She experienced some initial feeding difficulties and was discharged home from the nursery at 5 days of age. As a toddler, Jane was mildly delayed in acquiring gross motor developmental milestones, but she was more significantly delayed in acquiring fine motor and adaptive developmental milestones. She began receiving private occupational therapy (OT) services at 18 months of age. Jane's mother reported persistent current concerns about Jane's fine motor and adaptive development, reporting that she is unable to unbutton, button, or tie her shoes. She reported that at school, Jane has difficulty with handwriting and drawing, and she has had a particular academic difficulty in math. She also reported that despite not exhibiting delays in her acquisition of speech and language developmental milestones, having a large vocabulary, and being able to relate experiences verbally, Jane has trouble with back-and-forth conversation. She reported that Jane frequently makes tangential comments, and she tends to have one-sided conversations, where she will repetitively list facts about her restricted interest in insects, without acknowledging whether others are listening or paying attention to her. She reported that Jane also tends to take things very literally, and she has difficulty recognizing humor and sarcasm. Jane's mother reported that Jane exhibits behavioral rigidity, with a strict need for routine and an overfocus on rules, and she often tattles on other children for breaking the rules. She reported that Jane prefers to play by herself, and she does not have any friends at school or in her neighborhood. She reported that Jane has no difficulties with inattention, impulsivity, or hyperactivity at home or at school. On physical examination, Jane was found to have short stature, webbing of her neck, and a low posterior hairline.During the DBP evaluation, Jane was observed to exhibit poor eye contact, to have difficulty modulating the volume of her voice, and to engage in one-sided conversations. On developmental testing, Jane received a standard score of 72 (age equivalent of 4 years, 6 months) in visual-motor integration on the Beery-Buktenica Developmental Test of Visual Motor Integration. On the Kaufman Brief Intelligence Test-2, she received a verbal standard score of 121 and a nonverbal standard score of 88. On the Wide Range Achievement Test-5, she received a Word Reading standard score of 129, a Spelling standard score of 126, and a Math Computation standard score of 74. Based on the history provided by her mother and direct observations of her behavior during the DBP evaluation, on the Childhood Autism Rating Scale, Second Edition, High Functioning Version, Jane received a score of 34, placing her behavior in the severe symptoms of autism spectrum disorder category. Given her physical examination and the results of her developmental evaluation, genetic testing was pursued, and Jane was found to have Turner syndrome (monosomy X).Based on her diagnosis of Turner syndrome, Jane was determined by her school district to qualify for an Individualized Education Program under the category of "Other Health Impairment," and she was provided direct OT services and accommodations for math. She was not qualified to receive special education services under either the "Autism" or "Specific Learning Disability" categories, as it was concluded by her special education team that her medical diagnosis of Turner syndrome accounted for all of her special educational needs.What diagnoses need to be included in the DBP report, and what education does the medical team need to provide the special education team regarding the relationship between etiological and developmental diagnoses for children with developmental disabilities?

titre: Biceps rerouting and derotational radial osteotomy: A technique for correcting forearm supination in NBPBP.
auteurs: Patel Arsh N, Gaviria Manuela, Sabbag Casey M
resume: Forearm supination deformity is a recognized late sequela of neonatal brachial plexus birth palsy (NBPBP) that can impair functional positioning of the hand and limit activities requiring forearm pronation. Surgical options include forearm osteotomy, tendon rerouting, tendon transfer, and combined procedures. We describe a modified technique combining derotational radial osteotomy with biceps tendon rerouting using cortical button fixation. This was a single-patient technical case report. An 18-year-old male with longstanding fixed forearm supination deformity secondary to NBPBP underwent radial derotational osteotomy and biceps tendon rerouting. The biceps tendon was detached with the forearm in maximal supination, rerouted through the interosseous space, and secured with a cortical button with the forearm in maximal pronation. A radial osteotomy was subsequently performed toward pronation with approximately 30° to 45° of rotational correction. Postoperative rehabilitation included protected immobilization followed by progressive range of motion and strengthening. Preoperatively, the forearm rested in approximately 15° of supination, with active pronation limited to neutral and active supination to approximately 50°. Following surgery, the forearm rested in approximately 15° to 20° of pronation. Passive forearm rotation improved from 45° of supination to 40° of pronation preoperatively to 60° of supination to 75° of pronation postoperatively. At 12 months, active pronation improved from neutral to 55° of pronation. No postoperative complications were reported during follow-up. The patient participated in occupational therapy 1 to 2 times weekly during recovery. This case demonstrates the technical feasibility of combining radial derotational osteotomy with biceps tendon rerouting using cortical button fixation for longstanding supination deformity following NBPBP. The technique provides an additional fixation option for tendon rerouting while addressing the underlying osseous rotational deformity. Given the single-patient design and absence of comparative or biomechanical data, further study is required to determine whether cortical button fixation offers advantages over established tendon fixation methods and to evaluate the reproducibility and clinical efficacy of this approach.

titre: Effects of Incorporating Horses into Occupational Therapy on Adrenocortical and Sympathetic Nervous System Reactivity and Regulation in Autistic Children: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
auteurs: Rankins Ellen M, Aichele Stephen, Granger Douglas A, Hepburn Susan, Gabriels Robin, Schmid Arlene A, Peters B Caitlin
revue: Journal of autism and developmental disorders
resume: The study prospectively investigated adrenocortical and autonomic nervous system reactivity and regulation as autistic children participated in a randomized controlled trial of occupational therapy in an equine environment (OT-Equine). Autistic children (n = 72, ages 6-11 yrs) were randomly assigned for 10 weeks to OT-Equine or clinic-based occupational therapy (OT-Clinic). Saliva samples (later assayed for cortisol and alpha-amylase, [sAA]) were collected before (pre-session), during (within-session), immediately after (post-session), and 20-minutes after (post-session + 20) each 1-hour weekly session. Data were analyzed with a generalized linear mixed-effects model. Across the 10 sessions, pre-session sAA significantly increased (exp(b) = 1.02 per week, p < 0.05). Within sessions, sAA increased (exp(b) = 1.22; p < 0.01) during therapy and recovered post-session + 20. Group differences in sAA changes were non-significant. By contrast, pre-session cortisol concentrations were stable across the 10-weeks (exp(b) = 1.01; p > 0.05). Within session, however, cortisol concentrations decreased from pre- to post- and post-session + 20, with greater reductions among OT-Equine participants (exp(b) = 0.77; p < 0.01). Changes in cortisol were associated with improved treatment outcomes. The pattern of reactivity and recovery in sAA suggests that children experienced autonomic/sympathetic arousal in response to therapy sessions, perhaps associated with excitement and positive affect. Moreover, stable pre-session cortisol concentrations across sessions for both groups, and declining cortisol concentrations within sessions for the OT-Equine group, suggests OT-Equine participants also held subjective experiences characterized by familiarity and low levels of distress. Taken together, findings suggest the integration of horses into occupational therapy for autistic children creates an exciting positive therapeutic environment, associated with improved treatment outcomes. The study was registered as a clinical trial at clinicaltrials.gov (NCT05846932, registered April 26, 2023).

titre: Assessing the effectiveness of podcasts in supporting occupational therapy career readiness.
auteurs: Kubiak Abbigail, Jacobs Karen, Kulkarni Varsha S
resume: BackgroundPreparing occupational therapy students for emerging practice areas (E/IPA) requires scalable strategies to build career readiness beyond traditional clinical training. While podcasts show promise for career exploration, their efficacy in fostering OT career preparedness remains understudied.ObjectiveTo evaluate how podcast interventions enhance OT students' career readiness by improving awareness, confidence, and perceived competence in emerging and innovative practice areas (E/IPA).MethodsA cohort study (N = 87 OT students) used pre/post surveys including the Perceived Competence Scale (PCS) and researcher-designed Likert scales. Mixed-effects linear regression was used to model the odds of improvement in interest, awareness, confidence, and competence, and to examine demographic associations.ResultsPodcast exposure was associated with significant increases in awareness, confidence, and competence relative to interest. First-year OT doctoral student listeners demonstrated greater effects (awareness OR = 37.33). Gender effects were non-significant.ConclusionsPodcast content may support OT students' preparation for diverse career pathways by demystifying E/IPA roles and providing and providing affective and cognitive scaffolding for non-traditional practice areas. These findings suggest that podcasts can foster career adaptability and may help address inequities in access to role models and exposure to innovative practice. Integrating podcasts into curricula could enhance career readiness while equipping students to navigate healthcare's evolving landscape.

titre: Exploring rehabilitation therapists' knowledge and perspectives on the use of artificial intelligence and machine learning for persons post-stroke.
auteurs: Donoso Brown Elena V, Lee Min Hun, Stepansky Kasey, Fairchild Hannah, Mikula Kaia, Del Vecchio Mia, Halyama Robert
resume: BackgroundThe integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) within the clinical work of rehabilitation therapists in post stroke rehabilitation has the potential to transform their work performance, habits, and routines. The impact could potentially enhance integration of assessment/data analysis, personalizing therapies, documentation, and promoting home program adherence.ObjectiveThis study assesses occupational and physical therapists' current perspectives on AI/ML in post-stroke clinical rehabilitation and examines perceived barriers to potential application of AI/ML in their clinical work.MethodsThis mixed methods study includes quantitative survey data collected pre/post an AI/ML educational webinar, as well as qualitative focus group analysis that includes therapist attitudes and experiences with AI/ML, practical applications to using AI/ML, as well as the difficulties associated. The recruited therapists include occupational and physical therapy practitioners from the United States and Asia. Individuals included in the study had to have a caseload of 30% persons with stroke.ResultsFour key themes emerged from qualitative analysis: 1) current clinical work practice and identified gaps, 2) current therapists' perceptions of AI/ML, 3) perceived future of AI/ML in clinical work practices and 4) steps needed for implementation. Survey data reporting frequencies of technology use and AI/ML perceptions are integrated into qualitative findings.ConclusionsTherapists can articulate potential future uses for AI/ML technology in post-stroke rehabilitation, however, remain uncertain about when, how, and at what cost utilization will be supported in clinical work environments. Therapists desire education and support to utilize the evolving technologies in practice.

titre: Which Clinical Reasoning Models Are Used by Physiotherapists, Occupational Therapists and Selected Allied Health Professionals? A Scoping Review.
auteurs: Schultz Henry, Virgara Rosa, O'Callaghan Ellen, Aguilar Ali, Graham Kristin, Kumar Saravana
resume: Clinical reasoning is a critical skill for Allied Health professionals, enabling informed decision-making in patient care. While a wide variety of clinical reasoning models are taught across disciplines, it remains unclear which models are frequently applied in practice. The scoping review aimed to map the literature on clinical reasoning models used by allied health professionals. This review was informed by Joanna Briggs Institute's framework for scoping review. Searches were conducted across Medline, Embase, Emcare, SCOPUS, CINAHL, the Cochrane Library and gray literature sources in January 2024. Results were screened in duplicate and data were descriptive synthesized and summarized the clinical reasoning approaches reported in the included studies. Forty studies were included, spanning clinical reasoning literature from physiotherapy, occupational therapy, psychology, podiatry, speech pathology, and dietetics; no studies were identified for social work or exercise physiology. Hypothetico-deductive reasoning and pattern recognition were the most commonly reported models of clinical reasoning across the included studies, while three track reasoning and dual-process theory also featured across some professions. Seven additional models were also reported, though these were documented as isolated instances. While several clinical reasoning models are used by Allied Health professionals in practice, only a handful are commonly reported in the literature, particularly within physiotherapy and occupational therapy. This is despite Allied Health curricula and training programs drawing on a much broader range of models. Evidence for other Allied Health professions remain limited, highlighting a need for further research to determine whether these patterns hold more broadly. These findings suggest a need to reassess the teaching and application of clinical reasoning models within the professions studied. Further research, particularly with underrepresented Allied Health professions, can help identify preferences and drivers influencing model use in practice.
